beats.vo: This is a real vulnerability. It hid in a production service for seven years — leaking password hashes through an ordinary API. Every unit test passed. Every code review approved it. Here's how ReGrade, from Curtail, would have caught it on day one.

Tests check what you expect. You write an assertion for every behavior you can think of. But nobody writes a test for a bug they don't know exists — so the bugs you never imagined sail straight through. ReGrade works differently. It doesn't check expectations. It compares behavior.

Here's the trick: there's no version two. We run two identical copies of the same service, and record an ordinary test suite against the first. The tests make no security assertions — they log in, read a user, rename one. To record, we point them at ReGrade with a single environment variable. They pass, unchanged. Then we replay that traffic against the second copy — the very same code — and ReGrade finds fifteen differences.

In Claude Code, we ask it to walk us through the replay. The fifteen differences fall into three buckets: a login token, some timestamps, and a password field. The token and the timestamps are exactly what you'd expect to differ between two runs — a fresh session, a fresh clock. So we tell ReGrade: map the token, and drop the timestamps.

But look closely. The token and the password hash look alike — both long, random strings that change every single run. It's tempting to wave them both away as noise. That's the trap. One is a session token you can safely map. The other is a secret your users trusted you to protect. You can't tell them apart by the fact that they changed — you have to look at what changed.

We replay once more, with the profile. The token is mapped, the timestamps are gone — and one difference remains: the password field. A bcrypt hash, returned in an API response, from the rename endpoint. That's the leak — the shape of C-V-E twenty twenty-three, fifty-nine sixty-eight. ReGrade found it comparing the app to itself, from ordinary traffic, with no security test in sight.

Why did seven years of tests miss this? Because a test can only check what someone thought to assert. Detecting the unknown is a different capability — and it's the one ReGrade adds. So here's the question: if your existing tests could find the vulnerabilities they were never written for, what would they find?
